opus-5.5.text:
I think this question has become much sharper in the last few years. If you look at university purely as a place to transmit knowledge, then honestly, its advantage is shrinking fast. Almost any course you want, the lectures are online, the textbooks are online, and now you can sit with an AI that will patiently explain a concept ten different ways until it clicks. For a motivated learner, the raw information is no longer scarce.

So for me the value of university has shifted to the things that are still scarce.

The first is people. The most important things I learned weren't really from the syllabus. They came from being around classmates who were better than me at something, from arguing with them late at night, from seeing how a good professor actually thinks when a problem doesn't have a clean answer. That kind of tacit knowledge, the taste and the judgment about what's worth working on, is very hard to get from a video or a chatbot. You absorb it by being close to people.

The second is structure and pressure. Everyone says they'll learn on their own, but most people don't go deep without some external rhythm: deadlines, exams, a research group that expects something from you every week. University gives you a few years where struggling with hard things is your main job. That protected time is actually quite rare in life.

The third is a place to try and fail cheaply. You can join a lab, switch directions, start a project that goes nowhere, and it's fine. Nobody expects you to be productive yet. That freedom to explore is something I think people underestimate until they leave.

Where I think AI changes things is that students should stop treating university as the place where you passively receive answers. If the answers are cheap, then what matters is learning to ask good questions, to judge whether an answer is right, and to build something real. The students who will get the most out of university now are the ones who use AI to speed up the basics, and then spend the time they save on the parts only a university can give: the people, the hard problems, and the chance to find out what they actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response says university’s advantage in transmitting knowledge is shrinking because courses and textbooks are online and AI can explain concepts, making raw information less scarce.

r002.rationale: It describes learning from classmates who were better at something and from being around people with valuable judgment and expertise.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think the premise that university is mainly about transferring knowledge was already shaky before AI showed up. Lectures have been on the internet for fifteen years. What AI changes is that now you also have a tutor who will answer any question at two in the morning, patiently, for free. So if the only reason to go to university is to acquire information, then yes, that reason is mostly gone.

But I never thought that was the real reason. When I look back at my own time at school, the things that actually shaped me weren't in any syllabus. It was being in a room with people who were smarter than me, or just different from me, and realizing how narrow my own view was. It was having four years where society basically gave you permission to not be productive yet, to try things, to fail at them, and nobody held it against you. You can't download that. An AI won't give you that.

I'd also say university teaches you taste. Not facts, but judgment. Which problems are worth working on, what good work looks like, who you want to become. You learn that by watching people who have it, and by arguing with your peers late at night about things that don't matter. AI can give you answers, but it's actually not great at giving you questions. The questions come from friction with other human beings.

The other thing, and I think this is underrated, is that university is a filter and a network, and that's not a bad thing. The people I started companies with, the people I still call when I'm stuck, I met most of them in those four years. The density of ambitious, curious people in one place at one time is really hard to replicate.

So my view is that AI makes the bad parts of university, the memorization, the lecture as content delivery, obviously obsolete. And that should force universities to be honest about what they're actually for. The ones that double down on community, on mentorship, on giving young people space and ambition, will matter more, not less. The ones that are just expensive content platforms, I think, are in trouble. And they should be.

r001.rationale: The candidate says lectures have long been online and AI now provides a free, on-demand tutor, so university's role in providing information is mostly gone.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes learning alongside smarter peers and says university brings a dense community of ambitious, curious people who become lasting connections.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to separate the value of learning from the value of attending university. If your goal is to understand a subject or acquire a skill, AI and the internet give you many ways to do that. So universities can’t justify their value simply by saying, “We have knowledge, and you need to come here to receive it.”

But access to information isn’t the same as an education. You still need to learn how to ask good questions, judge competing explanations, and stay with a difficult problem. A good university gives you structure, feedback, and people who challenge your thinking. Your classmates can be as important as your teachers in that process.

So I wouldn’t say university has become unnecessary. I’d say its value is becoming more dependent on what actually happens there. Does it help you develop judgment? Does it give you opportunities to experiment and work with others? Or are you mainly collecting credits and a credential? AI makes that distinction harder to ignore.

r001.rationale: The response says AI and the internet offer many ways to learn and that universities can no longer justify attendance simply by providing knowledge, communicating that they have lost their former exclusivity in knowledge access.

r002.rationale: It says classmates can be as important as teachers and that people can challenge your thinking, but it does not clearly present valuable access to social connections with high-quality peers as a university benefit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to separate the value of learning from the value of attending university. If university is simply a place where someone explains information to you, then AI and the internet do challenge that model. You can learn a great deal without sitting in a classroom.

But university can offer something harder to create on your own: a community where people challenge your thinking, a structure that makes you work through difficult subjects, and opportunities to try things you wouldn’t have known to look for. A good teacher doesn’t just give you an answer; they help you recognize that you’ve asked the wrong question.

Of course, those benefits aren’t automatic. You can attend university and spend four years passively completing assignments. You can also learn independently and build a very serious intellectual community. So I wouldn’t say university is the only path. I’d ask: does this particular university, at this cost, help you develop judgment, relationships, and the ability to do meaningful work?

AI makes access to answers much easier. That makes the ability to judge those answers—and decide what is worth asking—even more valuable. I think that’s where university needs to prove itself.

r001.rationale: The response says AI and the internet challenge university’s role as a place that explains information and let people learn a great deal outside the classroom, conveying that universities no longer have exclusive access to knowledge.

r002.rationale: The response describes university as offering a community of people who challenge one’s thinking and valuable relationships, conveying access to intellectually engaged peers.
